rendered: The premise needs a correction: the Cyrene-based separation was not run at room temperature. The main process was run hot. The cathode scraps were stirred in Cyrene [1], and the cathode powder was recovered by hot centrifugation and hot filtration. The reason is that PVDF dissolves in Cyrene only at elevated temperature: the authors found it barely soluble below 80 °C[2], and the DSC data put dissolution near ~90 °C[3], so the separation must be kept above that range. Cooling to room temperature was used in other places. First, the hot supernatant containing PVDF and carbon black was cooled to room temperature [4], so that the PVDF/CB composite and the recycled Cyrene could be filtered off. Another use was room-temperature filtration as a control. Below the dissolution temperature PVDF precipitates out, so the room-temperature filtered powder kept PVDF on it, as the FTIR band at 871 cm^−1[5] showed. [6] This contrast with the hot filtration, which removed PVDF, is what the authors used to show that the separation temperature must be kept high.
